content: Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a disease that occur within a specific time period, typically one year. It can be quantified either as a proportion or as a rate. The incidence proportion, also known as risk, is calculated by dividing the number of new cases by the size of the population at risk. For instance, in a stable population of 1,000 individuals, if 28 people develop a condition over a two-year observation period, the incidence proportion is 28 cases per 1,000 individuals. The incidence rate, on the other hand, measures the number of new cases per unit of person-time at risk. Using the same example, the incidence rate would be 14 cases per 1,000 person-years, as the incidence proportion (28 per 1,000) is divided by the number of years (two). The use of person-time rather than just time accounts for situations where some individuals may drop out of a study. The term incidence is sometimes used as shorthand for incidence rate, though this usage is imprecise and can lead to confusion. It is important to distinguish incidence from prevalence. Prevalence measures the total number of cases of a disease in a population at a given time, whereas incidence reflects the rate at which new cases occur. Thus, incidence provides information about the risk of contracting a disease, while prevalence indicates how widespread the disease is. For example, consider a disease that takes a long time to cure and was widely spread in 2002 but whose spread was halted in 2003. In 2002, this disease would have both high prevalence and high incidence. However, in 2003, the incidence would be low because fewer new cases are occurring, but the prevalence would remain high due to the long duration of the disease. Conversely, a disease with a short duration may have a low prevalence but a high incidence. In general, diseases with short durations are better assessed using incidence rates, while long-lasting or hereditary diseases are more appropriately measured using prevalence rates.
